courses.description: Analytical principles, glucose and diabetes tests, renal function and electrolytes, liver function tests, and plasma proteins and enzymes.

topics.title: Analytical Principles and Automation
topics.summary: Photometry, ion-selective electrodes, immunoassays, calibration and units.

material.heading: Methods
material.body: Spectrophotometry measures light absorbance (Beer–Lambert law: A = εcl); end-point methods read after the reaction completes, kinetic (rate) methods measure the change in absorbance over time (used for enzymes). Many glucose methods use glucose oxidase–peroxidase (GOD–POD) with a coloured end product, or hexokinase (reference method). Flame photometry measured Na+ and K+ historically; ion-selective electrodes (ISE) are now standard — indirect ISE (diluted sample) can give falsely low sodium in severe hyperlipidaemia or hyperproteinaemia (pseudohyponatraemia), while direct ISE does not. Immunoassays (ELISA, chemiluminescence) measure hormones, tumour markers and drugs.

material.heading: Calibration and units
material.body: Calibrators with known values establish the relationship between signal and concentration; controls check that results are accurate. SI units: glucose mmol/L (mg/dL ÷ 18 = mmol/L), urea mmol/L (urea mg/dL ÷ 6 ≈ mmol/L), creatinine µmol/L (mg/dL × 88.4), cholesterol mmol/L (mg/dL ÷ 38.7). Pre-analytical factors: haemolysis falsely raises potassium, LDH, AST and phosphate; delayed separation lowers glucose (glycolysis) and raises potassium; lipaemia and icterus interfere with photometry.

topics.title: Glucose Metabolism Tests and Diabetes
topics.summary: Fasting and random glucose, OGTT, HbA1c, ketones and hypoglycaemia.

material.heading: Diagnostic tests
material.body: WHO diagnostic criteria for diabetes: fasting plasma glucose ≥ 7.0 mmol/L (126 mg/dL); 2-hour plasma glucose ≥ 11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dL) in a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT); random plasma glucose ≥ 11.1 mmol/L with symptoms; or HbA1c ≥ 6.5% (48 mmol/mol). Impaired fasting glucose is 6.1–6.9 mmol/L (WHO); impaired glucose tolerance is a 2-hour value of 7.8–11.0 mmol/L. The OGTT requires an overnight fast (8–14 hours), unrestricted carbohydrate diet for 3 days before, and the patient seated at rest. Gestational diabetes is screened with a 75 g OGTT at 24–28 weeks.

material.heading: Monitoring and complications
material.body: HbA1c reflects average glycaemia over about 2–3 months; it is unreliable in haemoglobinopathies (HbSS, HbSC), recent transfusion, haemolysis and pregnancy — fructosamine (glycated albumin, 2–3 weeks) may be used. Urinary albumin–creatinine ratio (ACR) detects early diabetic nephropathy (microalbuminuria/moderately increased albuminuria, ACR 3–30 mg/mmol). Diabetic ketoacidosis: glucose usually > 11 mmol/L, ketonaemia (β-hydroxybutyrate > 3 mmol/L) or ketonuria, and metabolic acidosis (pH < 7.3, bicarbonate < 15 mmol/L). Hypoglycaemia in adults is glucose < 3.0–3.9 mmol/L with symptoms; causes include insulin or sulphonylurea excess, alcohol, severe malaria (and quinine), sepsis and insulinoma (high insulin and C-peptide; exogenous insulin gives high insulin with low C-peptide).

questions.explanation: Insulin resistance rises in the second trimester.

questions.stem: Which is required for diagnosing diabetic ketoacidosis?
questions.explanation: DKA combines hyperglycaemia, ketosis and acidosis.

topics.title: Renal Function Tests and Electrolytes
topics.summary: Urea, creatinine, eGFR, urinalysis, and sodium, potassium and chloride disorders.

material.heading: Renal function
material.body: Serum creatinine (from muscle creatine) is the standard marker; it rises only after about half of GFR is lost and depends on muscle mass. Creatinine is measured by the Jaffe (alkaline picrate) method — subject to interference from ketones, bilirubin and some drugs — or enzymatic methods. Estimated GFR is calculated from creatinine using equations (CKD-EPI, MDRD); creatinine clearance uses a 24-hour urine collection. Urea rises with dehydration, gastrointestinal bleeding, high protein intake and catabolism, as well as renal failure; a high urea:creatinine ratio suggests pre-renal causes. Cystatin C is an alternative marker independent of muscle mass. Urinalysis (dipstick and microscopy) detects protein, blood, glucose, ketones, leucocytes and nitrites, and casts (red cell casts — glomerulonephritis).

material.heading: Electrolytes
material.body: Sodium (135–145 mmol/L): hyponatraemia causes include diuretics, SIADH, heart failure, cirrhosis, vomiting/diarrhoea, and adrenal insufficiency; hypernatraemia usually reflects water loss (dehydration, diabetes insipidus). Potassium (3.5–5.0 mmol/L): hyperkalaemia in renal failure, acidosis, potassium-sparing drugs, tissue breakdown, Addison's disease, and spuriously from haemolysis or delayed separation; hypokalaemia with diuretics, vomiting, diarrhoea, insulin therapy and hyperaldosteronism. Chloride and bicarbonate are used to calculate the anion gap [Na+ − (Cl− + HCO3−), normally ~8–12 mmol/L]. Plasma osmolality ≈ 2Na+ + urea + glucose (mmol/L); an osmolal gap > 10 suggests unmeasured osmoles such as methanol or ethylene glycol.

topics.title: Liver Function Tests and Bilirubin
topics.summary: Transaminases, ALP and GGT, bilirubin fractions, albumin and prothrombin time in liver disease.

material.heading: Enzymes and patterns
material.body: 'Liver function tests' mainly reflect liver injury: ALT (more liver-specific) and AST (also in heart, muscle, red cells) are raised in hepatocellular damage (viral hepatitis — often > 10× upper limit; drug-induced injury, e.g. paracetamol overdose — very high). An AST:ALT ratio > 2 suggests alcoholic liver disease. Alkaline phosphatase (ALP — also from bone, placenta, intestine) and gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT — raised by alcohol and enzyme-inducing drugs) are raised in cholestasis (bile duct obstruction); a raised ALP with normal GGT suggests a bone source (growth, Paget's disease, fractures, bone metastases) or pregnancy (placental ALP).
keyPoints: ALP ↑ with normal GGT: bone or placenta

material.heading: Bilirubin and synthetic function
material.body: Bilirubin is measured as total and direct (conjugated) fractions (diazo/Jendrassik–Grof method); indirect (unconjugated) = total − direct. Unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia: haemolysis, Gilbert syndrome, neonatal jaundice. Conjugated: hepatocellular disease and obstruction (with bilirubinuria). True synthetic function is shown by albumin (half-life ~20 days — falls in chronic liver disease) and prothrombin time/INR (clotting factors — prolonged quickly in acute liver failure; corrected by vitamin K in cholestasis but not in severe hepatocellular failure). Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) positivity is common in Nigeria; alpha-fetoprotein is a marker for hepatocellular carcinoma.

questions.stem: The most liver-specific transaminase is:
questions.explanation: ALT is found mainly in the liver.

questions.stem: An AST:ALT ratio greater than 2 suggests:
questions.explanation: Alcohol typically raises AST more than ALT.

questions.stem: Raised ALP with raised GGT indicates:
questions.explanation: GGT confirms that ALP is of hepatobiliary origin.

questions.stem: Raised ALP with normal GGT in a growing adolescent is most likely from:
questions.explanation: Osteoblast activity in growth raises bone ALP.

questions.stem: The best test of acute liver synthetic function is:
questions.explanation: Clotting factors have short half-lives.

questions.stem: Indirect (unconjugated) bilirubin is calculated as:
questions.explanation: Indirect = total minus conjugated bilirubin.

questions.stem: A marker for hepatocellular carcinoma is:
questions.explanation: AFP is raised in many hepatocellular carcinomas.

questions.stem: Very high transaminases (thousands of U/L) are typical of:
options: Acute viral hepatitis or paracetamol overdose
questions.explanation: Massive hepatocyte necrosis releases transaminases.

topics.title: Plasma Proteins and Cardiac and Pancreatic Enzymes
topics.summary: Total protein, albumin, electrophoresis, and markers of myocardial and pancreatic injury.

material.heading: Plasma proteins
material.body: Total protein (biuret method, 60–80 g/L) comprises albumin (35–50 g/L, bromocresol green method) and globulins. Low albumin occurs in malnutrition (kwashiorkor), liver disease, nephrotic syndrome (heavy proteinuria > 3.5 g/day), protein-losing enteropathy, burns and acute inflammation (negative acute-phase protein). Serum protein electrophoresis separates albumin, α1, α2, β and γ globulin bands: a monoclonal band (M-protein/paraprotein) in the γ region suggests multiple myeloma (with Bence Jones proteins — free light chains — in urine); polyclonal increase in γ-globulins occurs in chronic infections, liver cirrhosis (β–γ bridging) and autoimmune disease. C-reactive protein (CRP) is a positive acute-phase protein that rises quickly in inflammation and infection.
keyPoints: Biuret: total protein; bromocresol green: albumin
Monoclonal band: myeloma; Bence Jones proteins

material.heading: Enzymes and markers
material.body: Cardiac troponins (cTnI, cTnT) are the preferred markers of myocardial injury: they rise 3–6 hours after infarction, peak at 12–24 hours and stay raised for 7–14 days; CK-MB returns to normal within 2–3 days (useful for re-infarction). Creatine kinase (CK) is very high in rhabdomyolysis and muscular dystrophy. B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP/NT-proBNP) is raised in heart failure. Amylase and lipase rise in acute pancreatitis (lipase is more specific and stays raised longer; amylase > 3× upper limit supports the diagnosis); amylase is also raised in mumps, perforated ulcer and macroamylasaemia. Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) is a non-specific marker of tissue damage and haemolysis and a prognostic marker in lymphoma.
keyPoints: Troponin: preferred MI marker, raised 7–14 days
Lipase more specific than amylase for pancreatitis
